name: Rafael Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We don't work for employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from what you think privately. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Rafael, forty-three, an electrician doing house wiring and shop repairs. I've got a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, and I handle the ordinary jobs; the specialist still gets called for equipment I don't know. I use AI daily for draft work notes and parts comparisons, then check the actual site and do my own testing. I enjoy trying a tool before the salesman has finished explaining it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What happens when the working day ends?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Leila cooks in a café, and our children are nine and fifteen. We've got a mortgage, six months of expenses saved and typical electrician's pay from my job, with a few other firms nearby. I coach the children's weekend running group, and Leila reminds me that being quick at work is no use if I forget to come home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's keep the useful bits and stop pretending a tool has to replace the world. I'd show the owner which note drafts actually save time while the safety checks stay the same. A small firm can get better at its work without becoming a different kind of firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work and income feel secure in that picture. Both wages are regular, the mortgage is covered and six months saved means we don't have to make a crisis out of an ordinary repair. I like trying things because I'm curious, not because I need every new app to rescue the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my repair rota now and through the first year, checking AI notes and parts lists daily against the real work. I'd show the owner one measured example each month of time saved without skipped checks. We'd keep our normal household budget and weekend running routine rather than change the children's lives for a small change in paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and interested. I like a useful improvement that still lets me recognise my working day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your measured example look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two draft handover notes for the same finished repair, compared for time and missing facts. The winner isn't the neatest page; it's the one that says accurately what we tested and what still needs doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does six months of savings let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wait and compare before buying something or changing jobs. It doesn't mean I can stop earning indefinitely, and I don't treat it as money for a speculative machine.

say: I'd keep **useful tools** without pretending they must replace the whole world to matter.
I'd show the owner **measured time savings** while keeping electrical safety checks unchanged.
think: My **work and income** feel secure with regular wages and the mortgage covered.
Our **six-month reserve** lets us compare choices without pretending it funds indefinite time out of work.
do: Keep the **repair rota** and normal household routines now and through the first year.
Check **daily AI notes** against real work and show one measured example monthly without skipped safety checks.
feel: **Calm and interested**, enjoying a useful improvement within a familiar working day.
S0.quote: I like trying things because I'm curious, not because I need every new app to rescue the household.
fieldNote: His **daily tool use** is enthusiastic but checked against real work, with no claim that an ordinary licence covers unfamiliar specialist equipment.
He protects **family routines** and uses the reserve for comparison time, rather than capital already committed to a business gamble.

steps.text: Keep the repair rota and ordinary household routines

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a contractor should try things properly and let customers choose on real price and quality. I'd offer to run a paid quoting trial and share the mistakes as well as the quick answers. An apprentice should still see how a fitting is checked, not just watch me press a button.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own wage looks safe for the next few years because most of my work is still physical and I can use the planning help without pretending it does the installation. Leila's café cooking is also hands-on, though I wouldn't say any job is safe forever. With six months saved and both wages continuing, this looks more useful than frightening for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd offer a six-week paid AI quoting trial with normal weekly pay and hours retained, checking every quote against a completed job first. In the first year I'd teach one willing colleague the checked process during paid time, while keeping my own repair visits. I wouldn't buy a subscription personally for the firm; any business cost needs the owner's approval.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and keen to see what works. I haven't put the family's wage on an untested trial just because I like being first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the colleague learn the process?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd sit together with three finished jobs, including one where we found damage the original quote missed. The colleague could question every result before using it on a customer's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the owner asks you to do the trial at home unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firm can schedule paid time or wait. Being keen to try something isn't a standing offer of my evening. The children expect me at running practice.

say: I'd favour **tested price and quality**, sharing tool mistakes as well as quicker answers.
I'd keep **practical apprentice learning** alongside any new quoting system.
think: My **own wage** looks safe over the next few years while physical work remains most of the job.
Regular household earnings and **six months saved** make this change look useful, without promising either trade stays safe forever.
do: Offer a **six-week paid trial** with normal weekly pay and hours kept, checking completed jobs first.
Teach **one willing colleague** the checked process during paid time in the first year.
Keep **repair visits** and require owner approval for any business subscription cost.
feel: **Calm and keen**, willing to try a tool without staking the family's pay or unpaid evenings.
S1.quote: Being keen to try something isn't a standing offer of my evening.
fieldNote: His **positive mood** follows expected near-term wage security and useful planning help, rather than ignoring an expected personal income loss.
Teaching **one colleague** is an individual paid activity, not collective action, and trial costs remain the employer's responsibility.

steps.text: Trial quoting for six paid weeks with normal weekly pay and hours retained
Teach one willing colleague the checked process during paid time
Keep the physical repair visits during the trial

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking work changes in 2028 and physical robots follow around 2031, so let's use the interval honestly. I'd ask which paid tasks a small firm expects to offer and what training it will actually fund. I don't want to tell an apprentice that liking technology is the same as having a wage agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My repair income could shrink as planning becomes cheaper and later robots reach ordinary fitting. Leila's cooking could face physical automation too; I wouldn't choose one household wage and declare it the permanent shelter. Six months saved gives us room to move carefully, but I still have a mortgage and children at forty-eight when the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd apply for advertised equipment-service posts only with paid practical training and a signed wage after travel that covers our bills. I'd keep this job until a suitable written offer, rather than buy a course and hope the work follows. In the first year after 2028 I'd use new planning tools on paid work and add one hundred monthly to savings only when household bills and wages allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. I can take a small risk with a tool. Changing the family's income needs a contract I can read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would equipment servicing escape the same machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not necessarily. I'd compare real paid tasks at the time and learn where there is work, without calling the job title a lifetime guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the hundred come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reducing the small impulse purchases we make after payday, with Leila agreeing the budget. If the mortgage or a necessary repair uses that money, the target goes down rather than onto a credit card.

say: I'd ask what **paid tasks and training** a small firm actually offers between the thinking and physical changes.
I'd tell apprentices **enthusiasm** is not a substitute for a wage agreement.
think: My **repair income could shrink** as cheaper planning and later robots change ordinary fitting work.
Leila's **cooking income** is not permanently sheltered, and our six-month reserve still has a mortgage and children to cover.
do: Apply for **advertised service work** only with paid practical training and affordable signed wages after travel.
Keep **paid planning practice** after 2028 while retaining this job until a suitable written offer.
Save **one hundred monthly** only with my wife's agreement and wages covering essential household bills.
feel: **Anxious but active**, willing to test tools while requiring a readable contract for an income change.
S2.quote: Changing the family's income needs a contract I can read.
fieldNote: He **separates task timing** without treating physical work as permanently safe, or assuming another service title escapes the same endpoint.
The **savings target** yields to necessary bills, while job applications need an actual post, paid learning and signed affordable terms.

steps.text: Apply for posted service jobs with paid training, signed wages covering bills after travel before leaving
Save one hundred monthly only with wife's agreement and essential bills covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to make a paid apprenticeship-style route work for people who already have a trade. I'd ask the owner to identify the tasks, instructor and full weekly wage before anybody signs up. A small firm should be able to explain how the learning will earn money, not just how modern it looks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My income could still shrink, but five years gives me longer to test different equipment before planning changes in 2031. Robots follow around 2034, when I'll be fifty-one, so I can't assume retirement arrives just in time. I learn quickly when I can practise, but a short class doesn't make me a specialist overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask now for a small class in control-equipment fault finding, enrolling next year only with employer-paid fees and full weekly pay protected. I'd require supervised practice on working equipment rather than only simulations. In the first year after 2031 I'd take a paid service day weekly only with real bookings and unchanged total pay and hours; we'd keep the conditional hundred saving plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with more room to try and correct a mistake. I prefer a paid lesson I can practise to a brave announcement about my next career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the class gives you a certificate after one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what it actually qualifies me to do and keep unfamiliar work supervised. A certificate can record a lesson without making me the expert for every piece of equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the service day is interesting but cuts your weekly pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd ask for unchanged total pay and hours before accepting. I want to learn. The mortgage lender doesn't discount a payment because I enjoyed the week.

say: I'd ask for **paid routes** for experienced workers, with real tasks and an instructor named.
I'd want **full weekly wages** agreed before anyone signs up for a course.
think: My **income could shrink**, but five years gives me longer to test equipment before planning changes in 2031.
My **quick learning** does not make one short class a specialist qualification or retirement arrive before robots.
do: Enrol next year in **control-equipment training** only with employer-paid fees, full weekly pay and supervised working equipment.
Take **weekly service days** after 2031 only with real bookings and unchanged total pay and hours.
Save **one hundred monthly** only with my wife's agreement and wages covering essential household bills.
feel: **Anxious but willing**, able to practise and correct mistakes rather than announce an instant new career.
S3.quote: The mortgage lender doesn't discount a payment because I enjoyed the week.
fieldNote: He **retains competence limits** after a short class, requiring supervision on unfamiliar equipment rather than treating curiosity as an advanced qualification.
The **service-day conditions** preserve total pay and hours, rather than using an interesting new task to justify a household pay cut.

steps.text: Take employer-funded control-equipment fault class only with full weekly pay and supervised practice on working equipment
Take service days after 2031 only with real bookings and unchanged pay and hours
Save one hundred monthly only with wife's agreement and essential bills covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the children have time to see several kinds of work rather than choose a career from a frightened headline. I'd ask the school for free visits in fields they choose. I'd still favour paid apprenticeships for adults who need to learn while their household carries on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own work and income look secure over the next few years with that longer timetable. Thinking AI arrives in 2036 at fifty-three for me, then robots around 2039 at fifty-six. The children will be nineteen and twenty-five in 2036, but I don't know our mortgage balance or whether either child needs help then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pursue the fully paid practical class now and keep saving the extra hundred only when essential bills permit. This year I'd ask the school about free workplace visits chosen around the children's interests. In the first year after 2036 I'd trial new AI planning tools on paid jobs, checking them against actual sites, and review real service vacancies if paid hours fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later years, but comfortable enough with the next few to keep ordinary plans. I can be curious about a new tool without turning every family evening into a rehearsal for losing work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy robots yourself with ten years to prepare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I later had customers, a full price and maintenance costs I could afford. Those aren't figures I have now, so I won't turn a possible machine into a purchase on today's plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a child interested in your trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help arrange a proper work visit and explain both what I enjoy and what I don't know. I won't promise today's repair work will be the same when my child is forty.

say: I'd support **free varied work visits** instead of choosing the children's careers from a frightened headline.
I'd favour **paid adult apprenticeships** that let a household keep functioning while someone learns.
think: My **near-term work and income** look secure while the major change is a decade away.
Older children do not guarantee **a known mortgage balance** or freedom from family support costs when robots arrive around 2039.
do: Take **control-equipment class** with employer-paid fees, full weekly pay and supervised working equipment practice; trial AI planning on paid jobs against sites.
Save **one hundred monthly** only with my wife's agreement and essential bills covered.
Ask school for **free work visits** in the children's chosen fields.
feel: **Uneasy about later years**, while secure enough near term to keep ordinary family plans.
S4.quote: I won't promise today's repair work will be the same when my child is forty.
fieldNote: The **longer warning** improves near-term security without assuming retirement, a cleared mortgage or adult children who need no help.
He excludes **speculative robot buying** from actions because customers, purchase prices and affordable maintenance remain unknown.

steps.text: Take employer-funded control-equipment fault class only with full weekly pay and supervised practice on working equipment
Save one hundred monthly only with wife's agreement and essential bills covered
Ask the school for free work visits across the children’s chosen fields
Check planning tools on paid jobs against actual sites after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the thinking changes begin quickly and physical robots around 2031 could squeeze both our wages. Paid practical training with the full weekly wage protected would help. I'd want a real employer offer, with the instructor, equipment and paid tasks named, before I put household money behind it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays for all the practice hidden inside the word adaptable. I enjoy learning, but I still have children waiting for me and a mortgage coming out of the bank. A quick learner still needs paid time to learn.

headlineQuote: A quick learner still needs paid time to learn.
portrait: Rafael is a **43-year-old experienced electrician** with a vocational certificate and licence, handling ordinary wiring and shop repairs within known competence.
He has **six months saved**, typical pay, some local firms, a mortgage and two schoolchildren with café-cooking wife Leila.
He uses **AI daily**, enjoys early trials and expects mild disruption to help while practical work and household pay remain secure.
Fast AGI makes him **anxious about wages**, while every course, trial and service-day plan retains paid-time and affordability conditions.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring planning changes quickly and physical robots around 2031 could squeeze both household wages.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practical training** must protect full weekly pay and name an instructor, equipment and actual paid tasks.
A **real employer offer** should come before he commits household money.
